## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a reject-by-default policy for hostPath usage, a common attack surface, and to describe how to maintain a dynamic allowlist in production.

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- hostPath volumes and host filesystem access risk
- dynamic allowlist via a ConfigMap and a small controller to sync data
- CI validation (dry-run, gatekeeper admissions) and runtime validation

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: HostPathPolicy
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: HostPathConstraint
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package hostpathpolicy
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
        some i in input.review.object.spec.volumes
        input.review.object.spec.volumes[i].hostPath
        not data.hostpath_allowlist.namespaces[_]
        msg := "hostPath volumes are forbidden unless in allowlist"
      }
```

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: HostPathConstraint
metadata:
  name: hostpath-deny
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: ["v1"]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
```

Compliant manifest (no hostPath):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.23
```

Noncompliant manifest (hostPath present):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: noncompliant-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: data
    hostPath:
      path: /var/lib/data
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.23
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /data
      name: data
```

CI/runtime validation plan: run Gatekeeper admission checks on PRs, simulate allowed namespaces via the ConfigMap sync, and perform a runtime audit post-deploy using a test pod to verify policy enforcement.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests advanced policy enforcement for image provenance in multi-cloud Kubernetes deployments, including runtime verification via canary tracing.

## Key Concepts
- OPA/ Gatekeeper policies for image provenance
- Docker image digests and container labels
- Canary tests and distribution across clouds
- End-to-end tracing with OTLP and trace-id linkage

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal Deployment manifest snippet
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: feature-service
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: feature-service
        data_version: v1.2.3
        model_version: v0.9.7
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: feature
        image: registry.example.com/feature-service@sha256:abcdef...
        imagePullPolicy: Always
```

```yaml
# minimal GitHub Actions snippet (validation)
name: Validate Provenance
on: [push]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Inspect image for digest and labels
        run: |
          CONTAINER_IMG='registry.example.com/feature-service@sha256:abcdef...'
          DIGEST=$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' $CONTAINER_IMG | cut -d'@' -f2)
          LABELS=$(docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Labels}}' $CONTAINER_IMG)
          if [[ -z "$DIGEST" || "$LABELS" != *data_version* || "$LABELS" != *model_version* ]]; then
            exit 1
          fi
      - name: Canary trace test
        run: |
          # pseudo-step: send request and verify OTLP trace propagates
          curl -sS http://feature-service.canary/health -H 'traceparent: 00-abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789-1234567812345678-01' >/dev/null
          # verification would query OTLP collector for trace-id
          echo 'Canary test passed'
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this for high churn and lineage drift?
- What are the trade-offs of strict label enforcement vs. flexibility across teams?
- How would you simulate cross-cloud network latency in the gate?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to extend supply-chain security beyond images to function artifacts, and to integrate artifact attestations with a central provenance store in a multi-cloud serverless context.

- Cosign signing for containers and function artifacts
- Dependency attestations (dep-attestation) linked to a provenance store

## Code Example

```javascript
// Minimal pseudo workflow outline (Kubernetes-admission flow not shown)
name: Sign Artifacts and Gate
on: [push]
jobs:
  sign_and_gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Sign container image
        run: cosign sign ghcr.io/org/app:tag
      - name: Sign function artifact
        run: cosign sign artifacts/org/app-wheel-0.1.0-py3-none.whl
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: syft ghcr.io/org/app:tag -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
      - name: Rekor attestations

```

- What metrics would you monitor to detect signing failures or provenance drift?

## Why This Is Asked

Real-world cross-cloud serverless platforms demand automated image signing and artifact attestations. This question tests end-to-end workflow design, policy enforcement decisions, and practical CI/CD integration skills.

## Key Concepts

- Cosign signing and verification
- Rekor attestations for transparency and auditability
- SBOM generation (using tools like Syft)
- Multi-cloud serverless deployment patterns
- GitHub Actions workflow integration

## Code Example

```yaml
name: cks-serverless-sign
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3

      - name: Set up Syft for SBOM
        uses: anchore/syft-action@v1

      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }} -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json

      - name: Sign image with cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign --key cosign.key ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Verify signature
        run: |
          cosign verify --key cosign.pub ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Upload to Rekor
        run: |
          cosign upload blob -f attestation.json
```

## Failing Manifest (Unsigned Image)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: serverless-workload
spec:
  containers:
  - name: function
    image: registry.example.com/serverless-fn:abc123
```

## Passing Manifest (Signed Image)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: serverless-workload
spec:
  containers:
  - name: function
    image: registry.example.com/serverless-fn:signed-sha256
    imagePullPolicy: Always
```

## Local Verification

```bash
# Verify image signature
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/serverless-fn:signed-sha256

# Verify attestation
cosign verify-attestation --type cyclonedx --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/serverless-fn:signed-sha256
```

## CI Verification Steps

1. Add Cosign verification step in CI pipeline
2. Block deployment if signature verification fails
3. Verify SBOM matches image contents
4. Check Rekor transparency log for attestation
